title: Cosmoserve Raises $6 Million to Remove Space Debris, Opens Hyderabad Facility
headline: Cosmoserve Raises $6 Million to Remove Space Debris, Opens Hyderabad Facility
subheadline: The ex-ISRO founder's startup pairs a Rebright-led seed round with Base 1, a debris-removal test facility, and a retest of its failed first capture mission.
summary: The ex-ISRO founder's startup pairs a Rebright-led seed round with Base 1, a debris-removal test facility, and a retest of its failed first capture mission.
excerpt: The ex-ISRO founder's startup pairs a Rebright-led seed round with Base 1, a debris-removal test facility, and a retest of its failed first capture mission.
body:
• Hyderabad spacetech startup Cosmoserve Space has raised $6 million in a seed round led by Japan's Rebright Partners, taking its total funding past $9 million since it was founded last year.
  • The company inaugurated Base 1, which it calls India's first private space debris removal facility, in Hyderabad — with a rendezvous and capture lab, an ISO Class 8 clean room and a microgravity simulation platform.
  • Its first capture demonstration, Mission Embrace-1 aboard Skyroot's Vikram-1, saw its soft robotic petals fail to deploy; the company says it has identified the thermal cause and Embrace-2 follows in the coming months.
  • Founder Chiranjeevi Phanindra, who spent close to 15 years at ISRO, targets completing all technology demonstrations by 2027 and starting commercial operations by 2028.

Cosmoserve Space, a Hyderabad startup building spacecraft to remove defunct satellites and orbital debris, has raised $6 million in a seed funding round led by Japan-based Rebright Partners, Inc42 reported. Aranya Holdings and Naandi Ventures also participated, while existing investors AUM Ventures and Shakti VC increased their stakes. The round takes Cosmoserve's total funding to over $9 million, and founder Chiranjeevi Phanindra told Inc42 the company's valuation has doubled since its September pre-seed round.

What Cosmoserve is building

The startup's core technology is a soft robotic capture system — robotic petals designed to grip a dead satellite that has no docking point — paired with a vision-based navigation system. Its craft are designed to be refuelled in orbit so a single mission can remove multiple pieces of debris, rather than one object per launch. Alongside debris removal, the company is developing in-orbit satellite repair and refuelling technology.

A first mission that failed, and the fix

Cosmoserve's first technology demonstration, Mission Embrace-1, flew aboard Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 rocket to test the capture system, but the robotic petals failed to deploy as intended. Phanindra said the company has since identified and addressed potential issues with the thermal mechanism used to release the petals and the effect of low temperatures on the system. Embrace-2, an upgraded validation mission, is expected in the coming months, followed by a full-scale demonstration in which the company aims to approach within 10 metres of a dead satellite.

Base 1 in Hyderabad

Alongside the funding, Cosmoserve inaugurated Base 1, its Hyderabad facility for designing, building and testing satellite servicing and debris recovery missions. Phanindra described it as India's first private facility of its kind and the world's sixth equipped with space vision effects and microgravity simulation; it cost around ₹6 crore to construct. The site houses an orbital rendezvous and capture lab, a space robotics innovation lab, an ISO Class 8 clean room for satellite integration, and a mission control centre. Union Minister of State for Science and Technology Dr Jitendra Singh and Telangana IT Minister D Sridhar Babu attended the inauguration. The company also plans to raise its share of local manufacturing from 60%, reducing dependence on imported optics, avionics and space-grade electronics.

The road to 2028

Phanindra, who served close to 15 years with ISRO before founding Cosmoserve in June 2025, said the company holds letters of intent from four satellite constellation operators — one from the US, one from Europe and two from India — whose dead satellites must be removed under regulation. "We are aiming to get one paid customer before actual commercial operations begin," he told Inc42. The plan is to complete all technology demonstrations by 2027 and start commercial operations in 2028. The company has also said its two spacecraft are designed to service up to 100 satellites, potentially bringing servicing costs down from about $10 million to below $1 million per satellite.
